-- Intelligence --

Of all things it is most ironic how people view intelligence. Not the idea of intelligence itself, but its embodiment. We all look the same, we all have the same parts, so how dare this person think of himself better than me? Unsurprisingly strength, body building, these have far larger groups and are never particularly disparaged for their athleticism. Yet if you get an intelligent human, one of the first things they realize is how utterly hated you are if any conclusions reached contradict the hierarchy of fellow humans. Call yourself intelligent, or prove it by example and dare admit to it, and the hordes of unwashed masses come to ensure you know your place. Call yourself strong, lift twice your body weight to prove it, and praises abound around you.

Psychologists, neurologists, biologists, people in psychometrics, nobody agrees on a functional definition of intelligence. If you ask someone in psychometrics, the "G factor" is what matters, even though studies in neurology and later statistical analyses reveal working memory alone dictates some 80% of the weighted G factor. Do people accept this? Evidently not. Academia has an ongoing war in each of its "buckets", and psychologists who study the behaviors of the intelligent generally find their lives are rarely any better for their intelligence however defined. Rather socioeconomic status at birth dictates, in spite of intelligence, their probable outcomes. The inherent contradictions discovered in our expectations of the intelligent, and our means to measure them, has resulted in fissures even in the laymen and popular science. Anything from declaring intelligence "doesn't real" (I am frankly mocking this position outright) to declaring different "kinds" of intelligences that fundamentally misunderstand functional divisions of cognition. There must be "social intelligence", and "emotional intelligence", and "street smarts" (to make the illiterate feel better).

These are not fissures limited in popular junk science, for even when looking up papers in psychology you find such descriptors. I could ironically remark that the people advocating these arbitrary distinctions are more upset they are inadequate to the task and letting the common speech infiltrate their good sense. For, as previously mentioned, in spite of the arbitrary further ill defined divisions of "intelligences" none of them serve as predictors of outcomes dissimilar from socioeconomic status. Therefore, as a descriptor it is of dubious use, and as a predictor it's functionally meaningless. One more recent exemption to this rule is the functional dichotomy presented between crystalline intelligence and "wisdom", but more on that later.

It is of greater irony that people are "surprised" when studies of groups like the "Termites" reveal they fare no better than the median, excepting income. They're more likely to have particular cognitive biases, more likely to believe in the paranormal. This doesn't give credibility to the suggestion that human thought affects outcomes in reality, but it does reveal that intelligent people are so used to their locus of control being beyond that of median individuals they extend it to other elements of reality. If you are exceptional and only exist with normal, is it really surprising you formulate a model of reality that hints at something "beyond" explicable?

What's more, it's self evident that if you are a giant in a land of midgets you are less likely to acquire skills. You don't have to. This is one element of the cognitive elements in humans not acknowledged when it is discovered "wisdom" tests are more often failed by individuals of higher IQ's. While they would more rapidly learn the cognitive skills involved when challenged, the fact is society does not challenge them. Society is composed of the median, for the median, and anyone above that median doesn't have to perform beyond those boundaries. In other words, intelligence can be a victim of its own success, while at the same time become disparaged by those successes if they admit to their intelligence being the cause. The result? A new inquiry into the effect of trained "intelligence humility" which, to nobody's surprise, simply mimics the innate idea proposed by Socrates in the search of true wisdom. When there's nobody to challenge you pragmatically, you must be taught to challenge yourself. Which education system does this? None, because the average individual already finds life sufficiently challenging to not bother himself by self-doubt. Contrariwise the intelligent individual finds life so simple as to not need to bother himself by self-doubt.

So intelligent people are not, at least if Baltes "Berlin Wisdom Paradigm" is correct, generally more wise than others in practice. This of course lead to the "realization" (of some two thousand five hundred years ago) that wisdom is something which can also be trained, and thus people of intelligence will succeed faster when challenged. While a lot of papers have been published in recent years attempting to explain this none of them come to the simple conclusion of "because they don't have to be". This not only underpins a fundamental flaw in the cognitive faculties of the intelligent, but of every human being due to the nature of our cognitive processes. Without challenge and with the greater ability to avoid challenge, periphery skills atrophy below that of the norm. Just as, in the case of bodybuilders, they might not have any skill in actual fighting because they've never "had to".

There is a simple functional way to think about it. Intelligence is ones ability to solve abstract problems, while wisdom is ones ability to solve pragmatic problems. While ones ability to abstract the pragmatic does mean greater facility to achieve wisdom faster, it simultaneously means one doesn't have to. In fact the more successful one is in the abstract the less likely it is for that individual to require solving of pragmatic problems by simple fact of their extreme success in the singular faculty of the abstract. Again, it is the giant who doesn't need to learn how to fight because nobody can challenge him, and is thus taken down by a boy with a sling that nobody dared throw at him before.

-- Society --

All of this necessarily follows from a simple idea. The intelligent are not challenged pragmatically in a society that innately favors the median, because it is constructed by (and for) that median. Worse, they're challenged for the wrong reason: An intelligent person (by plethora of online anecdotes) faces continual workplace disappointment as they more rapidly attain the skills employers assign arbitrary "years of experience" to for higher progress in that career. If someone of exceedingly high intelligence attains those skills in one year, or even half a year, do you imagine they find it fulfilling to remain the next six years? Not in the slightest. It is of no surprise, then, that people of higher IQ's trend toward changing jobs or careers at far higher rates than others.

It is the innate hierarchy of society itself that makes intelligent people less than what they could be. Even worse, for both normal and intelligent individuals, there's no impetus to self doubt. While the Dunning-Kruger effect reveals that intelligent persons are more likely to accurately estimate their ability (or even underestimate it), the self estimation by normal individuals greatly exceeds their capacity.

The above can be taken to task for its details, but the details are largely irrelevant to the reasoning and crux of the matter. For once you have an intelligent individual who is capable of abstract and pragmatic self-actualization, they become the ultimate loser in the game of life. This is because, as life is composed only for the challenges of the median, everything is innately unfulfilling when that's all people expect of you. Worse still, by exceeding those expectations intellectually you receive mere adulation by the few who idolize such feats, with the innate realization that such adulation is purposeless to your own cognitive progress.

Therefore I conclude with the expectation that any such self-actualized individual will, by these designs, be like the giant of a man who is also very successful in combat. Not only would nobody fight him, but if someone does and he wins nobody is surprised. Nobody would reward this person. Nobody would care. The more successful you are in the realms of cognition in all of its faculties, and the more recognize you are for it, the less you "get out of it" in any meaningful capacity.

In other words, if Superman really did exist and had no equivalent supervillains, the only time anyone would even begin to appreciate him is in his absence. Worse yet, any such individual so far beyond the capacity of the norm would inevitably break the norm so badly as to transgress the laws of the land. While this is easily visualized in physical strength, as would be Superman being prosecuted for damages or under prohibitions of vigilante justice, the inevitable transgressions of such an intelligence would lead them to "crime" by definition. For the conceptions of justice are of the norm, and not the exceptional.

Thus, if anyone is truly looking for the brightest genius on the planet by combination of cognitive faculties, he is far more likely to have been to prison for a victimless crime than not. Far more likely to be disenfranchised by his fellow man than not. Far more likely to not care about success than not. For, in the end, the only winning move is not to play with pigeons, but also to admit you're never going to truly know your capacity (and remain indefinitely unfulfilled) when you do.

Thank you for reading.

No intellectual challenge whatever? Maybe imagine living in Idiocracy for a relative comparison.

Finally, I would remark that people of exceptional giftedness often become "flunkies". While some excel, others choose not to. If you listen to their stories you will hear time and again that they never learned how to tackle something once it is challenging.
